cemc-hypatia-2017-01a.title: Inscribed angles
cemc-hypatia-2017-01a.body:
$\angle BAD$ subtends arc $BCD$ and $\angle BCD$ subtends arc $BAD$; the two arcs make the whole circle ($360^\circ$), so the inscribed angles add to $180^\circ$: $2u = 92$, $u = 46$.

**Answer: 46**

cemc-hypatia-2017-01b.title: Use both quadrilaterals
cemc-hypatia-2017-01b.body:
In cyclic $STQR$, $\angle SRQ$ is opposite $\angle STQ$: $x + 58 = 180$, so $x = 122$.

In cyclic $PQRS$, $\angle SPQ$ is opposite $\angle SRQ$: $y + 122 = 180$, so $y = 58$.

**Answer: $x = 122$, $y = 58$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-01b.title: Same arc
cemc-hypatia-2017-01b.body:
$\angle SPQ$ and $\angle STQ$ are inscribed angles on the same arc $SQ$ (both $P$ and $T$ are on the same side of $SQ$), so $y = 58$. Then $x = 180 - 58 = 122$ from $STQR$.

**Answer: $x = 122$, $y = 58$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-01c.title: Isosceles triangles
cemc-hypatia-2017-01c.body:
In $\triangle JKL$, $KJ = KL$, so $\angle KLJ = 35^\circ$ and $\angle JKL = 110^\circ$. Opposite angles: $\angle JML = 180^\circ - 110^\circ = 70^\circ$. In $\triangle JLM$, $LJ = LM$, so $\angle LJM = 70^\circ$ and $w = \angle JLM = 180 - 140 = 40$.

**Answer: 40**

cemc-hypatia-2017-01c.title: Arcs
cemc-hypatia-2017-01c.body:
Inscribed $\angle KJL = 35^\circ$ means arc $KL = 70^\circ$; $JK = KL$ gives arc $JK = 70^\circ$. Then $\angle JML$ (on arc $JKL = 140^\circ$) is $70^\circ$, and in isosceles $\triangle JLM$ the apex angle is $w = 180 - 2 \cdot 70 = 40$.

**Answer: 40**

cemc-hypatia-2017-01d.title: Opposite angles and a straight line
cemc-hypatia-2017-01d.body:
$\angle DGF = 180^\circ - z^\circ$ (opposite $\angle DEF$ in the cyclic quadrilateral). Since $F, G, H$ are collinear, $\angle DGH = 180^\circ - \angle DGF = z^\circ$.

**Answer: $\angle DGH = z^\circ$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-01d.title: Compare two supplements
cemc-hypatia-2017-01d.body:
Both $\angle DEF$ and $\angle DGH$ are supplementary to $\angle DGF$ (one by the cyclic quadrilateral, the other by the straight line $FGH$). So they are equal: $\angle DGH = z^\circ$. (An exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.)

**Answer: $z^\circ$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02a.title: Use the square counts
cemc-hypatia-2017-02a.body:
After 5 rows, $5^2 = 25$ integers have been written, so the 25th integer is the last in Row 5. Row 5 ends at the 5th odd integer, 9.

**Answer: 9, in Row 5**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02a.title: Write it out
cemc-hypatia-2017-02a.body:
Row 5 is $1, 2, \ldots, 9$. Rows 1–4 contain $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16$ numbers, so the 25th number is the 9th in Row 5, which is 9.

**Answer: 9, in Row 5**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02b.title: End of Row 10
cemc-hypatia-2017-02b.body:
$100 = 10^2$, so the 100th integer ends Row 10, which ends at the 10th odd integer $2 \cdot 10 - 1 = 19$.

**Answer: 19**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02b.title: Count rows
cemc-hypatia-2017-02b.body:
Row $n$ has $2n - 1$ entries; rows 1 through 10 have $1 + 3 + \cdots + 19 = 100$ entries. The last one is the largest entry of Row 10, namely 19.

**Answer: 19**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02c.title: Locate the row
cemc-hypatia-2017-02c.body:
$44^2 = 1936 < 2017 \le 2025 = 45^2$, so the 2017th integer is in Row 45, which ends at $2 \cdot 45 - 1 = 89$ (the 2025th integer). Going back $2025 - 2017 = 8$ places gives $89 - 8 = 81$.

**Answer: 81**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02c.title: Count forward
cemc-hypatia-2017-02c.body:
Row 45 starts with the 1937th integer, which is 1. The 2017th integer is the $(2017 - 1936)$th $= 81$st entry of Row 45, which is 81.

**Answer: 81**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02d.title: First appearance
cemc-hypatia-2017-02d.body:
Row $n$ contains $1, \ldots, 2n - 1$, so 96 is in Row $n$ exactly when $2n - 1 \ge 96$, i.e. $n \ge 48.5$, so $n \ge 49$. Rows 49 to 200: $200 - 48 = 152$ rows.

**Answer: 152**

cemc-hypatia-2017-02d.title: New numbers per row
cemc-hypatia-2017-02d.body:
Each row repeats the previous row and adds two new numbers (an even and the next odd). Row 49 ends at 97, adding 96 and 97; Row 48 ends at 95. So 96 first appears in Row 49 and stays in every later row: $152$ rows out of the first 200.

**Answer: 152**

cemc-hypatia-2017-03b.title: Find the line
cemc-hypatia-2017-03b.body:
At $x = 4$ the parabola has $y = -16 - 12 = -28$. The line through $(0, 8)$ and $(4, -28)$ has slope $-9$: $y = -9x + 8$. Intersecting: $-9x + 8 = -x^2 - 3x$, i.e. $x^2 - 6x + 8 = 0$, $(x - 2)(x - 4) = 0$. So $a = 2$.

**Answer: $a = 2$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-03b.title: Product of roots
cemc-hypatia-2017-03b.body:
If the line is $y = mx + 8$, the intersections solve $-x^2 - 3x = mx + 8$, i.e. $x^2 + (3 + m)x + 8 = 0$. The roots are $4$ and $a$, and their product is $8$, so $4a = 8$ and $a = 2$.

**Answer: $a = 2$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-03c.title: Slope through two points
cemc-hypatia-2017-03c.body:
The points are $(p, -p^2 + kp)$ and $(q, -q^2 + kq)$. The slope is
$$\frac{(-p^2 + kp) - (-q^2 + kq)}{p - q} = \frac{-(p - q)(p + q) + k(p - q)}{p - q} = k - p - q.$$
The line is $y = (k - p - q)(x - p) - p^2 + kp$; at $x = 0$: $y = -kp + p^2 + pq - p^2 + kp = pq$.

**Answer: $pq$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-03c.title: Vieta
cemc-hypatia-2017-03c.body:
Let the line be $y = mx + b$. Intersections satisfy $-x^2 + kx = mx + b$, i.e. $x^2 + (m - k)x + b = 0$, whose roots are $p$ and $q$. By Vieta's formulas, $pq = b$.

**Answer: $pq$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-03d.title: Substitute and factor
cemc-hypatia-2017-03d.body:
Substitute $y = -x^2 + kx$ into $x = \frac{1}{k^3}y^2 + \frac1k y$ and multiply by $k^3$:
$$k^3 x = (-x^2 + kx)^2 + k^2(-x^2 + kx) = x^4 - 2kx^3 + k^2x^2 - k^2x^2 + k^3x,$$
so $x^4 - 2kx^3 = 0$, i.e. $x^3(x - 2k) = 0$. The second point has $x = 2k$ and $y = -4k^2 + 2k^2 = -2k^2$.

So $T = (2k, -2k^2)$. With $x = 2k$, $y = -2k^2 = -\frac{x^2}{2}$. All points $T$ lie on $y = -\frac12 x^2$.

**Answer: $y = -\frac12 x^2$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-03d.title: Check a value
cemc-hypatia-2017-03d.body:
For $k = 1$: curve $x = y^2 + y$, parabola $y = -x^2 + x$. The point $(2, -2)$ satisfies both ($4 - 2 = 2$ and $-4 + 2 = -2$) and lies on $y = -\frac12 x^2$. In general $T = (2k, -2k^2)$, eliminating $k$ gives $y = -\frac{x^2}{2}$.

**Answer: $y = -\frac12 x^2$**

cemc-hypatia-2017-04a.title: Greedy, digit by digit
cemc-hypatia-2017-04a.body:
Start with 9. The second digit can't be 8: then the third digit would be smaller than 8, making $9 > 8 > c$, not a zigzag. Take 7, and then the third digit must exceed 7: it is 8. So the number starts $978$.

Now the pattern goes down–up: $8 > d < e$. From the remaining digits 1–6, the largest choice with $d < e$ is $d = 5$, $e = 6$. Next $6 > f < g$: $f = 3$, $g = 4$. Finally $4 > h < i$: $h = 1$, $i = 2$.

**Answer: 978563412**

cemc-hypatia-2017-04a.title: Verify
cemc-hypatia-2017-04a.body:
$978563412$: $9 > 7 < 8 > 5 < 6 > 3 < 4 > 1 < 2$ — alternating ✓. Any number starting $98$ fails (third digit makes $9 > 8 > c$), and after $97$ the third digit must be 8; at each later stage the chosen pair is the largest possible pair $d < e$ from the remaining digits with $e$ below the previous peak, so no larger zigzag number exists.

**Answer: 978563412**

cemc-hypatia-2017-04bi.title: Delete the first digit and relabel
cemc-hypatia-2017-04bi.body:
A number counted by $G(6, 3)$ has the form $3b\,cdef$ with $b \in \{4, 5, 6\}$, and then the pattern is $3 < b > c < d > e < f$.

Fix $b$. Delete the leading 3: the string $b\,cdef$ uses digits $\{1, 2, 4, 5, 6\}$ and satisfies $b > c < d > e < f$. Relabel by $1 \to 1$, $2 \to 2$, $4 \to 3$, $5 \to 4$, $6 \to 5$ (an order-preserving map). The result is a 5-digit number using $1, \ldots, 5$ with the same up/down pattern, so it is a zigzag number with first digit $b - 1$ and second digit smaller — counted by $L(5, b - 1)$.

Conversely, from any number counted by $L(5, b - 1)$, relabel $3, 4, 5 \to 4, 5, 6$ and put a 3 in front: the first digit is now $b$, and since $3 < b$ and the second digit is less than $b$, the new number is a 6-digit zigzag number counted by $G(6,3)$ with second digit $b$. These maps are inverse to each other, so the number of $G(6,3)$-numbers with second digit $b$ equals $L(5, b - 1)$.

Summing over $b = 4, 5, 6$: $G(6, 3) = L(5, 3) + L(5, 4) + L(5, 5)$. ∎

(Numerically both sides equal 14.)

cemc-hypatia-2017-04bii.title: Complement the digits
cemc-hypatia-2017-04bii.body:
Take a 6-digit zigzag number and replace each digit $d$ by $7 - d$. The digits are still $1, \ldots, 6$, and every inequality between adjacent digits reverses ($x < y \iff 7 - x > 7 - y$), so a peak becomes a valley and vice versa: the result is still a zigzag number.

If the original starts with $k$ and its second digit is greater than $k$, the new one starts with $7 - k$ and its second digit is less than $7 - k$. Applying the map twice gives back the original, so it is a bijection, and $G(6, k) = L(6, 7 - k)$ for $k = 1, \ldots, 6$.

Therefore
$$\sum_{k=1}^{6} G(6, k) = \sum_{k=1}^{6} L(6, 7 - k) = \sum_{j=1}^{6} L(6, j). \;∎$$

cemc-hypatia-2017-04c.title: Recursion for G
cemc-hypatia-2017-04c.body:
**Symmetry.** As in (b)(ii), complementing digits ($d \to n + 1 - d$) gives $L(n, k) = G(n, n + 1 - k)$, so the total number of $n$-digit zigzag numbers is $T_n = 2\sum_k G(n, k)$.

**Recursion.** As in (b)(i), removing the first digit $k$ (when the second digit is $j > k$) and relabelling gives $G(n, k) = \sum_{j > k} L(n - 1, j - 1) = \sum_{i = k}^{n-1} L(n-1, i)$. Using $L(n-1, i) = G(n-1, n - i)$:
$$G(n, k) = G(n-1, 1) + G(n-1, 2) + \cdots + G(n-1, n - k).$$

**Table** (start: the 3-digit zigzag numbers are 132, 231, 213, 312, so $G(3,1) = G(3,2) = 1$, $G(3,3) = 0$; also $G(n,n) = 0$):

| $n \backslash k$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 1 | 0 | | | | | |
| 4 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 0 | | | | |
| 5 | 5 | 5 | 4 | 2 | 0 | | | |
| 6 | 16 | 16 | 14 | 10 | 5 | 0 | | |
| 7 | 61 | 61 | 56 | 46 | 32 | 16 | 0 | |
| 8 | 272 | 272 | 256 | 224 | 178 | 122 | 61 | 0 |

(Each entry $G(n, k)$ is the sum of the first $n - k$ entries of the previous row.)

$T_8 = 2(272 + 272 + 256 + 224 + 178 + 122 + 61) = 2 \cdot 1385 = 2770$.

**Answer: 2770**
